asDecan.p: Your Sun sits in the first ten degrees of Capricorn, which on the calendar means you were born somewhere between the December solstice and New Year, while everyone else was on holiday. Each sign gets cut into three slices of ten degrees, and each slice has its own planet sitting on top of the sign's ruler. Capricorn belongs to Saturn, the planet of rules and time and doing things properly. Your slice is run by Jupiter, which is the planet of more. More room, more luck, more faith that it'll work out. The catch is that Jupiter is in fall in Capricorn. It's uncomfortable there and nobody really listens to it, so its generosity has to come in sideways, through a clever arrangement or a second job or a joke at the right moment. The Devil is your Sun card overall, and this is the finer grain inside it. The Three of Pentacles slice after yours has Mars in it and just grinds. The Four has the Sun and holds on tight. Yours is the one that keeps a pair of plans moving and somehow finds room.

You're the person who says yes to the second thing before the first is finished, and it mostly works, which is why you keep doing it. The Saturday you meant to rest turns into the market in the morning, fixing your mum's gutter after lunch, and a quote for a side job at the kitchen table that night. At work you're answering an email with one hand and sorting the roster with the other. When the budget comes up short, your first thought is never to cancel anything. It's to shuffle, move this bill to next fortnight, sell the bike, pick up a shift. Saturn in you wants a plan and Jupiter wants a bit of slack in it, so you plan with gaps. People find your calendar alarming. You find it quite relaxing, as long as nothing's actually sitting still.

Jupiter in fall gives you a kind of hope that's been through the books. You don't tell a friend who's just lost their job that everything happens for a reason. You sit down with them, look at the numbers, find the six weeks of runway they didn't know they had, and by the end of the night they're laughing about their old manager. Being cheerful and having actually done the maths is a rare combination, and people trust your optimism because they've seen you be gloomy about the right things. You're also good at timing, which gets less credit than it should. You can tell which job can hang in the air another week and which one has to be caught today, and you're usually right without being able to say how you knew.

The less obvious trap is that keeping both options going lets you avoid picking one. The job you half want and the business you half started. Staying in the city while pricing houses on the coast, for about four years. As long as both are moving nobody can say you chose wrong, including you. The other part comes from Jupiter being in fall. Pleasure doesn't sit easily with you unless it's earned and useful. A bonus arrives and within the hour it's gone on the car loan, and the weekend away gets pushed back again. You're generous with other people, often very, and then you keep a quiet tally of it that you'd be embarrassed to hear read out. Your partner can feel the tally even though you've never once mentioned it.

When something goes wrong, your first move is to add another ball. Somebody's in hospital and you're running the roster of who visits, still doing your job from the car park, and you've offered to cover the school pick-ups as well. It looks like coping, and for a few days it is. About a week in, the rhythm goes. You start dropping small things, a bill, a birthday, the thing you promised your kid, and you get sharp about it, with yourself first and then with whoever's nearest. The people around you can't find a gap to help, because every job has already been handed to you, by you. What helps is having one thing taken off you completely, handed over and out of your head, with someone you trust telling you it's gone. Then sleep, and a meal you didn't organise.

Born in the last stretch of December, a lot of people with this slice grew up with a birthday that got folded into Christmas. One present for both, a cake nobody had room for. It sounds small, but plenty of you learnt early to not ask for a fuss, and you carry that into love. You'll plan the anniversary down to the booking and then feel awkward being the one celebrated. You love by making room. You move a meeting to get to their thing, you rearrange a whole month so they can do the course. Your partner may not see how much shifting went into that, because you make it look easy, and then you're hurt they didn't notice. Tell them what it cost, lightly. And let them plan your birthday properly, on a day nowhere near the twenty-fifth.

Capricorn wants to build something that lasts, and the Jupiter in your slice wants it to grow. What you tend to end up with is a working life in two parts running side by side. The day job and the small business. The practice and the teaching. The steady contract and the thing you do on Thursdays that might turn into something. You're good in roles where the ground keeps moving, operations, logistics, events, running a café, anything with a budget and a deadline and too many people wanting things at once. Where you struggle is a job that's tidy and fixed, because you get bored and start inventing extra work. The Mars slice after you pushes through by force and the Sun slice digs in. You look for the angle. Keep a written list of what you've said yes to, and read it before agreeing to anything new.

At twenty this pattern mostly looks like hustle. Two jobs, a course, a band, a relationship fitted into the gaps, and a lot of pride in how much you can carry. Money's often tight and you're quite good at being broke, which is a skill in itself. Through the thirties the load gets real, a mortgage, maybe kids, a parent who needs more, and this is where people with this slice either learn to set things down on purpose or get taught it by a bad year. The ones who learn it tend to find Jupiter gets a bit more room, and some good luck arrives that they don't immediately put to work. By the fifties Capricorn has usually paid off the slow way it does, and the second thing you kept going all those years is often the one that turns out to matter. Most of you still keep a second thing on the go, just smaller ones.

Once a week, on the same evening, write every commitment you're carrying on one page, work and home and the favours you've promised. Then cross one off. It doesn't have to be the biggest. It has to be finished, cancelled or handed to someone, and you tell whoever's affected within a day. If you can't find one to cross off, stick the page on the fridge where your partner or housemate can see it and ask them to pick. Do this for a month and look at how the page changes.
